title: The spread of 18 published CPV width ratios does not require a sharp viewing-angle boundary
abstract: We test the narrow spread of published width-derived rotation ratios in 18 complex periodic variable hosts. We use verified aggregate statistics and an exact conditional noncentral chi-square law. With a linear log response and fixed Gaussian scatter, an unselected isotropic model gives p=0.011. The eight-star TESS subset gives p=0.067. A sharp-cut model has a one-sided 95% upper bound c=0.920 on maximum cos(i). The combined rejection reaches p=0.05 with response slope beta=0.713, or with smooth selection weight sin(i)^k at k=0.683, varied separately. Stronger smooth selection at k=5.07 matches the population variance without a hard angle boundary. This does not identify a real survey bias or remove the matched spectral-width excess. It shows that the spread alone does not locate a unique occulting plane. Small samples, fixed independent Gaussian errors and uncertain width response limit inference. Code, aggregate evidence, input hashes and repeat steps are included. No external record table is bundled.

display.caption: Lower-tail spread probabilities under a sharp angle cut, a response change, and smooth inclination selection. These are separate sensitivity models with fixed Gaussian scatter. The sample splits share stars.

citations.reason: Uses verified sample sizes and log-ratio spreads. Tests how strongly the spread alone constrains an angle boundary when response and selection assumptions change.
Matched width evidence and calibration-range limits motivate response sensitivity. No star-level data are reused.
